projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with John Kim was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: We are recording at the La Verne Community Center on December 17, 2001. Okay, for the record, what is your name?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: John H. Kim.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: What is your age currently?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: I'm 77 -- I can't remember my age. 77, yeah, 77.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Okay, where were you born and raised?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: In Honolulu, Hawaii.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: What is your family background? Do you have any brothers or sisters?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: See, my parents came from Korea back in the early 's and they got married in about 19 -- I'd say about or something like that, and then they had four children; that's my sister Bessie, myself, brother Kenny, and -- no, I think it was the other way. My sister Gracie first and then my brother Kenny, so there was four of us, and then my father died when I was about 12, and then, let's see, then my mother remarried couple years after that, and she married a ex-Navy man who was a guy named Albert Dixon Donahue, so I had a step-father who was Irish, and they had a son named Lee, they named him Lee, and so I have a half-brother named Lee, and currently at the time as we speak he's chief of police of the ?Pomona? Police Department. My two sisters, meanwhile, have passed away, and there's just my two brothers and myself right now.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: What was your educational background?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Well, I went to, like it says on the application, high school in Hawaii, and when I went on to Europe, I got my discharge there because I got my Dear John while I was there, so I stayed there as a civilian, but while I was in the Army there, I took extension courses with the University of Maryland, and even after I got discharged there, I continued classes with the University of Maryland, and I took general courses, nothing specific, so I got -- at least I got my German language class out of the way, four semesters. Being in Germany made it easier so I could get straight A's all the way through my, you know, German classes. Fact, it was the only classes I got straight A's through. Then I came home, continued taking evening classes at the University of Hawaii, and, see, meanwhile I got married while I was back in Hawaii. Then I came back to California. About that time, see, I had to get a job here because the jobs weren't that great in Hawaii, couldn't find a job there because I was in the engineering field. Back while I was in Hawaii, I was working with a sugar company building sugar cane machineries, doing part of the design work with other engineers, and then I came to California. I worked for a private company that was in the farming, you know, business, they made farm machinery, so that company came with was in Stockton, and we designed different machineries for different farm work like almond-hulling plants and _______ machinery, even the harvesting machinery and the planting machinery, and also with the -- with the other orders as they came in, different types of equipment, like tomatoe planters and potato harvesters and sugar beet harvesters, various different, you know, farming-type equipment that are all mechanized, and California is pretty well mechanized in their farm business and they use a lot of machinery. Even at that time they were using a lot of farm workers, but machinery was coming into use and then we were getting more and more of them, so I was getting involved more of that, and then the company went bankrupt because the factory workers went on strike and they, I guess they just killed the company and then had to find new work again, and I got a job with the U.S. Forest Service, so I put application in there, and I started off with the equipment development center here in San Dimas, and I went to work for them, and right off the bat I was working with firefighting equipment, fire trucks and pumpers and stuff like that, and so I got involved in a lot of fire equipment work, and then there were also different type of work like in the deserts where they have different type of landscape there where most of it is just sand, just desert, and they try and put them to use by planting grass out there, so we developed a machinery that prepared the land for that type of work and they were able to grow grass out there, and then the Bureau of Land Management used that land to lease out to cattle ranchers to graze the cattle out there, so they were able to put the land to some use that way, and also like the forest has some unique type of areas where ordinary machinery that you buy off the factories, you know, like farm equipment, they're not suitable, so we have to design special equipment for them, so that's what I got involved in, more and more of that type of work, even harvesting forest trees, you know, for making lumber or even pulp wood and stuff like that, so different ways you get, you know, like trees that are growing up in the mountains, there's no way of getting at them and be a lot of cable type of getting the logs off the mountain into the areas where they can process them. In the old days they used to just pull all that stuff down into the rivers and float them down to the -- to the processing plants, but more and more trucks are getting involved so more and more trucking equipment was used, so there were more roads built by then, and they got to the point where so much of it is getting road equipment and public was getting a little concerned and objecting to all that type of work up here, so the Forest Service, they have to work according to all of the public and get involved because the more they protest, the more they have to cut back, and they had different type of processing with what they call clear-cutting, where they cut a whole section out, take the whole section of trees out, and they re-plant in there and that way the trees got a better chance of growing because the sun would get to them and they can grow better, or they have select harvesting where they go out and pick certain trees and get them pulled in and leave the young ones there, but then becomes very expensive and the lumber costs more money and all that sort of thing, so a lot of controversy on that, didn't know what to do, and, in fact, still today they still have that argument of which is best, one way or the other, and this is all the way back through Alaska, even the different islands, Peurto Rico and Hawaii, and but they don't have so much forest areas as they do on the mainland of U.S., but most of it's concentrated, in fact, in the western states rather than eastern because eastern is mostly smaller trees and different type of trees where they are used more for wood pulp and they use it for, you know, other applications mostly for like newsprint or for paper that they need for books and things. That's what they do over there, but anyway, that was the type of work I was getting involved in until I retired about 16 years ago, and I haven't done anything because I tried to do consulting work, but it's -- it's not so simple as people think. They think you just stand around and do consulting work, because you have got to put your knowledge into areas that they need, and, you know, once you retire, you know, you don't get paid -- people don't pay much attention to you, they don't listen to you, so that's the problem, and that's what I was getting to, and so my education came more into that type of experience. In fact, I even got my registration for agriculture engineering with the state of California because I got so much of it that I grandfathered into it, so I didn't have to take a test or anything like that. I got enough engineers backing me up so they can say, yeah, you did all that work.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: What was your -- what was your wife's name and wartime occupation, what did she do?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: My wife is Theresa Kim. Actually she was originally Chung Ja Quan (ph), that was her maiden name, and she came to Hawaii when she was about 28, and she was visiting her aunt. Her aunt had a beauty shop in Hawaii, so she came visiting her then, and about that time I was in my 30's, and my mother was getting anxious to marry me off, you know, settle down, and, you know, being an old bachelor, I just -- I didn't save any money. I just, you know, enjoyed my life and just do what I wanted to do because I knew I -- anyway, we had an apartment building in Waikiki, and I got involved more in that with my mother, you know, taking care of it, and it was more like a -- almost like a fixer-upper because it was a lot of work had to be done on it, and I did it all on my own because I didn't have any help. My -- my younger brother Lee was just a kid then, you know, in high school, and my older brother -- I mean the brother below me, Kenny, was living here already. He was married and living in California, so, you know, he couldn't help me, so I was there by myself doing all that work, and that -- that's how I was considered as the most eligible bachelor then, and my mother was just anxious to get me married; short, fat, pimples, ugly, whatever, you know, she grab any woman that was available that she think she could fix me up with. Main concern she had was to marry me off and settle down, you know, raise a family, you know, kind of routine, and I wasn't ready to settle down anyway because I had to get my wandering days out of my system yet, you know. I still -- in fact, even as I worked with the Forest Service, I was traveling, you know, I was all over the country, and even after we got married, when I finally married -- we named her Theresa by the time we got married because she had to get an Anglican name, so Theresa was ideal, we thought, so she got Theresa, and we got married in Hawaii, and then right after we got married we came here. That's when I took a job at the -- in Stockton with that private company, and then we --

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: When was this about, when you married?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: 19 -- well, I was 39, and she was 28. In fact, she was considered an old maid by then, you know. In those days, you're 28, you're an old maid. So that would be like 1950 -- no, '63, '63 -- in 1963, because she came over in February and the match made as soon as she came over. In fact, my mother had gotten -- she had worked up a tactic where she _______ me to write to her before she came to act as a guide for her when she comes here to help her out when she comes to Hawaii, to get acquainted with Hawaii, so that's how I got to know her anyway ahead of time, and so when she finally came, we met, and I said, okay, I guess I'll get my mother off my back, and, you know, so we got married, and right away we came here, and in about September, October, and we settled in Stockton because it's where I got my job, and we had our first boy there, named him Alex, Alex, and then later when I had to get another job with the Forest Service, came here, and we had Dexter, that's our second boy, so Alex and Dex, and _______ -- fact, they lived there all their life in the La Verne area, and when we finally settled here in '72, when we bought this house we live in now, and we stayed there, we didn't, you know, we didn't go anywhere, just stayed there because I thought if I'm raising a family, I better stay put, I can't be traveling all over because in the beginning, when I first got married, went from Hawaii to Stockton, and then when the company went bankrupt, I got my job at the Forest Service, moved down here, and a couple of years later we moved back up north again, and I got a -- I got transferred to San Francisco, called it the regional office, and I worked there, and then couple years there they wanted me back here, so I said on condition I don't work for my previous supervisor because, you know, we never got along; we came down here, and then at that time I thought, well, I've got to stay put, you know, I don't want to transfer around anymore. Anyway, I had a good enough rating as a GS-12, and you know in the government employment GS-12 is in the upper range anyway, so don't bother, so we stayed here ever since and then the boys grew up here then, see, but I -- what I did was to keep my wanderlust going I bought a -- in the beginning we got the, like tents, you know, and took the boys when they were kids around tenting. Then I bought a -- what they call it a pop-up trailer, where you open it up into a tent, tow it with you, and so we towed around with that for a while, and I think about the time when they were in high school, high school age, and then we bought a camper that you mount on the back of a truck, had one of those for a while, so we traveled around and did that for a while. In fact, made one trip that was kind of funny because I left my wife in the service station and forgot all about her because she went in the restroom without telling us and we went about 60 miles before I realized that she was still back there, and so we had to come all the way back. That was from (?Needles?) to -- Arizona the first town was -- what was the first town there? There's nothing in between, you know, for 60 miles, and we had to haul her all the way back and pick her up and go back and that was a trip where we went all the way to Wisconsin because I had to go to a training session in Wisconsin, so we went all the way there, and then we took them places that we traveled where the kids could see the country and that's how I traveled, but on my job I was also traveling because I had to go to different places, in the forest mostly, and test the equipment and do whatever ________ and work that I had to put into my reports and people were -- as we developed the machines for the application, you know, application we had to put them into, so that was all the traveling and training. I did all of that stuff when I was young, but the kids, actually, anyway, meanwhile, I got them through that and I got them to college. Alex graduated from Cal Poly in Pomona and Dexter went to USC, U.C. Santa Barbara, and then he traveled a lot too. He got the wanderlust out of me, probably, because he went to Europe, you know, after he graduated, for one year and traveled all over Europe, 14 different countries, and came back home and he went to USC, got his Bachelor's in filmmaking, so now he's working for this magazine, they call it "Written By." It's scriptwriters' guild, you know, in Hollywood. That's what -- he's assistant editor now with that magazine. And he likes the work. He likes to write. Even when he was in school, you know, always liked to write. Newspaper, school newspaper, you know, things like that, and that was just my family life anyway, doing all those things.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Okay. Where were you on December 7, 1941?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: I was just getting out of bed about 7:00, a little before that, getting ready to go to church, and I had worked that summer and I bought one of those, we call it Chevy touring -- you know, you see in the movies where they got those old cloth-type, you know, cars, open around on the sides, that type, you know, for the gangster movies and all that, that type of car, anyway, and it was called a Chevy touring van. I bought one of those things. I was just ready to go to church and then I put on my -- see, I was putting on my tie and then I heard this booming sound out there, and my stepfather, we called him Don then, Don was outside working in the -- under his car. He was out there fiddling around, and I yelled out to him. I said, I think they're having maneuvers out there again." He says, "Yeah," and he stuck his head out and looked up there. He says, you know, being in the Navy, so he knows more or less what that type of event was all about, so he said, "Yeah, they using life ammo too." It's all black out there, and, you know, smoke coming out, and then he scooted back underneath and continued working, so I didn't think much of it either, so I was just in my car and I drove down to the town, downtown (?Ewa?) and just about the time when I got in front of the governor's mansion, because there was one spot in there where they had for the governor's home there, you know, it's a big old house, and I got right in front of it and something fell in front of me, I don't know whether it was a bomb, small bomb or artillery shell or something, but right in front of me, so I turned right around and went back home and said, yeah, we're at war all right, and then it came on the radio that -- Franklin Delano Roosevelt was president, and he said that we are being bombed by the Japanese, and he said this is the day of infamy and we were declaring war with Japan, you know, and right away Congress jumped on the bandwagon, they all said, yeah, you know, we're at war. That's it, that's how it all started with me, anyway. I was still in school, in high school, so but anyway, they closed the schools, declared martial law right away, you know, and we were under the military then, and so nothing we could do, you know, we were at war, so close all the schools, and every day for the first couple of weeks, you know, there would be sirens going, you know, and mostly false alarm because they thought the Japanese were going to come back and invade, you know, and none of that happened, and they took off and went back to Japan or wherever they were going, and but that was the day of the war for me when it started, and then later on they put us to work. They said school is off so able-bodied kids, especially high school kids, can do all the work, you know, and so I went to Pearl Harbor. The first thing I did was go to Pearl Harbor to work because Pearl Harbor needed a lot of help to build those ships up and repair the ships so that they could go back to war and fight the war with Japan, and, you know, they had bombed over a hundred ships then, and we had to go down there and a lot of them had to be raised out of the water and they stayed -- they stayed underwater and then, you know, all those bodies still in the water and still in the ships, they had to be cleaned out and they had to be, you know, I guess, tagged or checked out to see who the individual was so they can get records straight, so that was what was going on, but my job mostly was to work. Being small, so they put me in small spaces and popping rivets, you know. In those days, you know, there wasn't a thing as safety considerations because I had no ear protection, nothing when I go behind a bulkhead to pop the rivets because they didn't do too much welding on the ships those days and once those bulkheads anyway, were welded, you know, so -- I mean, not welded, but riveted, and that was my job to pop rivets, you know, and at the end of the day I would come out and I would be deaf, couldn't hear anything, and it got to the point we were working, I would guess, about hours a day and it would be seven days, every day, no holidays, no days off, nothing, unless you were sick or something, you know, otherwise you just continued working, so that was my first year there when I was working there when I was supposed to be in school but the schools were closed, so, and then anyway, that lasted for about a year and then they said, you know, you can go back to school because they are opening them back up again, so I went back and finished out high school, but that was the start for me, you know, with Pearl Harbor, and I don't know which is worse, out there fighting a war or working on the ships, but it was tough, you know, no fun, no fun there at all, but, yeah, we did a lot of work on the ships, and my stepfather at that time was working in Pearl Harbor, and he was a -- some kind of materials inspector or something like that, so he and I would go to work together, in the morning, before the sun comes up, you know, had to start heading for work and he -- and my experience, I'd say, was the most in-depth experience as far as starting to go to work was in that time, time period, because after that and before that, it was -- it wasn't all that so deep and, you know, work the type of thing I had to do because this was the one constantly, you know, you don't -- you always think in your mind that you're doing this for the country, we're at war now, so that's how you think. You don't think anything else, oh, I'm doing this crappy job and all this other stuff; you don't think like that. You just thinking that, you know, there's guys out there fighting a war and everything else and, you know, and at least you do something to help them out, because once you build the ships up and put them out to sea and they go off and fight the war again, and the ones that get damaged out in the sea, they come back to Pearl Harbor because we are the closest base for, you know, the ships to come back. It's a long ways to go to, like, San Diego or those ______ + then was Long Beach also, and whatever ports we have here, you know, there were two, three thousand miles at least they have to travel. They can't do that without losing the war, you know, they have to stay right here and fight the war, so that was the experience at that time for me anyway.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Just out of -- were you ever discriminated against for being Korean? Were you --

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: To tell the truth, in those days we didn't even think about discrimination, but I know a lot of my high school friends of Japanese-American ancestry, they, you know, they were there -- when the war started, first thing the FBI did was put out an executive order to round up all the Japanese-Americans and put them in these relocation centers, and I didn't even know about that, you know, because they don't tell us. You don't know what's going on. All I know is that my friends in school, the ones that were Japanese-American ancestry, they knew that this was, you know, something is going to happen to them, so they volunteered and formed what they call the 442 Combat Brigade and that was what started their volunteerism for them anyway to go out and prove that they are Americans, they are not Japanese, so they formed that, and I didn't know what was going on. All I know was that they were doing this, and for what, I didn't know either. I know they were going out there going into actual combat, and you know, when you think you're in high school and you're going off to fight a war right off the bat and start shooting somebody, you know, you got kind of mixed feelings, you don't know what to think, but these friends of mine, anyway, they volunteered, most of them. They went out there, and then later on, we started getting news, you know, from various sources that they were out there fighting a war in Italy and then, you know, they continued on through Europe, and a lot of them got killed and lost their arms or legs and, you know, whatever, and they were completely crippled, you know, they can't do anything, and they became the most decorated unit in the U.S. Army for the Second World War, so that's what eventually news came out. I didn't hear about it then because I meanwhile had volunteered myself, and by the time the war ended in Europe, so I was going over there and lots of them going home to stay and I'm going out to stay, you know, just opposite direction, so I didn't hear from any of them because they were coming this way, I'm going that way, and only way I can get the news, my family writing to me or telling me about it, whatever, so that's the only way I knew about those guys doing that, and now, in fact, my wife keeps asking me, "What happened to all your high school friends?" Because she writes to, you know, and keeps in touch with her high school friends. I said, "I don't have any." I don't know where they are because most of them got killed, you know, I mean, in the war or crippled or, in fact, one of the guys is Dan Inouye, Congressman in Hawaii, Senator in the U.S. Congress now, he was one class above me.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Oh, really.

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: So he lost an arm, you know, he got one arm missing, but he was in that 442 Brigade, and I met another guy here, but he didn't come from Hawaii, he was in California, and I had to do part-time work selling cars because I was a mechanical engineer and, you know, knew about machinery, I thought I would try selling cars, and I met this guy named Kusloki (ph), Japanese fellow, and when he heard that I had been in the war and during wartime over there and all that, so he kept in touch with me, but the only guy I knew, but he was not from my, you know, school days. He's just somebody I met later on, that we, you know, got to know about each other.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Did you personally know Dan Inouye?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Dan Inouye?

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: I really didn't know him because he was one class above me, and you know how it is in school, you know, you got one class above you, you think the class below you is, you know, dummies, whatever, nerds, that kind of thing, so, no, the ones I knew about I lost touch of because, you know, I moved around quite a bit. In fact, I got discharged in Europe, and I lived in Germany and I lived in Austria and I lived in Italy, you know. I was moving around, so, and I was working for the -- for the Quartermaster Corps in spare parts supply, and I was more interested in mechanical engineering type of work anyway, but it wasn't engineering work, but it was the supplying of it, getting spare parts, mostly, spare parts that had to be -- at first they were just cannibalized off the equipment that were already there, but later we started getting parts from the mainland U.S. shipped over there, so I had -- I initiated this, you know, the spare parts supply system coming from here going to Europe because I had handled the spare parts supply by cannibalizing off the old equipment, so I got involved in that to a point where eventually we ran out of that type spare parts so we had to get it from the mainland, and that's how I got that thing started and so I got, I don't know how many millions of dollars, but it was growing so fast that I got to a position where I was auditing of accounts then. I had to go travel all over Europe and European commands and audit the accounts and keep track of all the spare parts, where they are going, what they are doing with them and that sort of thing, and then I went like from the command in Germany, I went over to Austria, started working with them on their end of it because they were starting new route where the ports in Italy were being used as the -- as the entrance port for bringing stuff to Europe, the southern end of Europe for the Army, instead of bringing it all in one place and shipping it all over Europe, where they got it coming from the other end too, so I got involved later on. That's why I ended up in Austria and Italy, getting more that end of it involved where they're building up the system to do that, so that was my involvement in spare part supply in the military, mostly _______.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: You first joined the Navy in 1942?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Why did you do it?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Well, because they just said -- they told us the schools are closed and we're under military court mar -- martial law, and high school age, you have to get a job, go to work. Since I wasn't of Japanese ancestry, I was able to go to Pearl Harbor because they wouldn't hire anybody that was that Japanese ancestry. They think they were going to sabotage, sabateurs, and, you know, that kind of thing, so couldn't get a job there as a Japanese. I don't know about now, they probably changed the regulations, but at that time you couldn't. And Pearl Harbor was the only place where they needed a lot of working people. In fact, what they did was they got a lot of people from here, from the mainland and sent them over to work over there because I met a lot of those guys coming over from the mainland, coming over to Pearl Harbor to work because they needed a lot of people that can work on ships, repairing ships and know a lot about ship-type work than anything else, and that's where I got started. I worked at Pearl Harbor. I didn't have much of a choice, in other words.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: You just -- you just understood -- you were enlisted?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: What I did at first I was going in to work as civilian. Then eventually when I became of age where 18, you know, and over and I had to sign up for the draft, and instead of drafting us, the Navy grabbed us because they didn't want us to be drafted into the other military branches, so they got ahold of us and kept us in the U.S. -- they put us in the U.S. Navy Reserves, so they put us in there so they could keep us in Pearl Harbor to keep working, so that's how I got stuck in the Navy. Without even thinking about it I was in the Navy.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: How long were you -- you were working on the ships at Pearl Harbor for the Navy? How long were you doing this work?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: See, the high school, like I said, the first year. Then I went back to school, finished my schooling, and right after I finished my schooling, I went back again, and then for two years I worked in Pearl Harbor. In fact, at that time when I went back, because then I was 18, so I was working as a -- actually in the Navy Reserves, you know, because they had us locked in that way because U.S. Navy Reserves, so I stayed there, like it or not. I was in the military, you know. We didn't even wear uniforms or anything like that. On the record, that was it. In fact, I even got a serial number. Now, they talk about veteran's privileges or, you know, whatever, according to the law that you can have certain things, you know, you can apply for, whatever. That counts, too, for me because I was in the -- and that was during the wartime, so that was Navy, serial number, got my discharge papers and everything. In the Army, you know, I got the same thing, got my discharge papers, so I got two discharges, so like now, like Disneyland and -- what's that other place? Oh, Queen Mary (ph) and Knott's Berry ph), you know, they have Veteran's Day where veteran's can go in free if you show your discharge papers, so I can use it for that too, you know, so certain privileges you can have because you got the discharge papers. In fact, I even had a G.I. Bill of Rights loan that I could use. I used it only once, can use it only once anyway, so I used it once when I was in Stockton and we bought our house there, so I used it then. You know, at that time, when I bought that house, it was no down payment on the house. Just got this veteran's loan, and the payments were really small, small pay, $185 -- no, it was even less, around there, would take care of the principal and interest. As I say, there was no down payment, but principal, interest, and insurance, and I think it was property tax, all of that was included, it was, and that area where we bought into, even the water bill was cheap because we paid only one dollar a month. I don't know about now, but at that time, it was one dollar a month, and we were barely struggling to make ends meet because my paycheck was less than $600 a -- yes, less than $600 a month, and so, you know, inflation, now it's way up there somewhere, but at that time it was like that, so didn't have to pay much, but we managed, you know. In fact, I (?owned?) my car for about the next three years, but, you know, my wife didn't even know anything about that stuff because she just came here to this country and she was ignorant of all these things, and I think she had to learn English too, you know, go to English classes and all that, get her citizenship papers. She did all right when she went there.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: When you were working in the Navy in Pearl Harbor, were there any memorable moments?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Well, boy, it was nothing but drudgery work, I can say. It was hard work, period. I never worked so hard in my life, you know, jobs that I was in, but, see, the only thing that really stuck in my mind was that as we brought the ships up was all the dead bodies on the ships and the stench, you know, the smell was really -- in fact, this guy, this kid that was working up there, he was a football player, and he couldn't come to work the next day because the smell got to him, it was so bad. The dead bodies in there, you know, that had to be cleaned out and all that, and that was really bad. That was the most -- because you never forget that. You can't explain, you know, to somebody what it felt like or it smelled like, you know, because it's dead, period, you get to -- you get to experience that feeling that, you know, the smell and the -- practically the taste of the air, you know, was so bad, but, you know, when a person is dead, you would be surprised how smelly he can get, but that was it, you know, it was really bad. We learned these things, and you never forget it, you know, it's embedded in your mind forever, and the only thing is, like I said, when I first went there, for the first year, I was just a kid, and I never seen anything like that, you know, where these things were done, and seeing that -- it was almost like being in combat and somebody gets shot next to you, but you don't get to experience later on when the guy's dead and his body is rotting there and all that stuff, you don't get that experience. You get after, you know, because the body has to be there like for at least a month or something like that. Then you get that, you know, that atmosphere. It's a different kind of feeling like someone being shot, I guess, because I never got in that situation where I had to worry about somebody being shot or me being shot, because when I went in the Navy they never gave us any experience with firearms or -- but in the Army they did. We had to go to basic training and do that target practice and all that kind of thing, so, you know, I don't know why we did it because we never used it anyway. I never saw a rifle after that.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: When and why did you change from the Navy to the Army?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Because when I -- when the war ended in Germany, they didn't need anymore combat troops in Germany anymore, so then drafted people in the Army to go there to fight a war but as occupation forces. The Navy couldn't keep us because they told us that we were no longer considered as essential, you know, because the Navy and Army -- the Navy had almost won the war in Japan already anyway, so all of that was kind of ______, but they needed more and more men to go to like especially Europe, you know, as occupation forces, and there was a lot -- I almost got drafted -- in fact, I got my draft notice, but I went down to the recruiting office anyway and I volunteered. I said, you know, I want to pick that because you get a choice of which command you go to, so I said I want the European Command, so that's how they sent me to Europe instead, and I ended up in -- in fact, I had second thoughts when I got there. What the hell did I do? You know? Because it was the coldest winter, and being from Hawaii, you know, suddenly you're in the middle of winter, and, you know, and snow on the ground about a foot high, and, you know, you say, am I nuts coming here? And I mean, you were freezing and we didn't have any heating either, you know, that was it. In fact, throughout the transport like on the ship or being shipped to Europe, you had to use cold salt water to shower, so nobody showered, you know, they was -- they said that was ridiculous, so everybody stunk, you know, real bad. I mean, it was body odor everywhere, and then when we got there, we didn't have hot water, we didn't have anything, and tents were cold, and some of us thought we had heat because these pot-belly stoves in each tent, but there was no coal, so we couldn't heat up our tents, and what I did finally, I said, aha, I'm going to go to church every week because it was the only tent that was heated was the church. END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE BEGIN SIDE TWO, TAPE ONE

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: -- and then there's nothing under but bare floors, so _______ for a week getting to our next destination we called repple depple, replacement depots, so we had to go to a different depot and from there get transferred again and on, you know, so nobody took baths all that time, and you were dirty as can be, so and, you know, America is so used to taking baths all the time, so you get in a situation where you got to find somewhere to take a bath, so a bunch of us went to the local stream that's flowing through a town and we went in that ice cold water and we tried and take baths and these Germans are standing around there looking at us, dumb Americans, look what they're doing. So it was -- it was something. It was an experience. We went at least cleaned up parts of our bodies because there was no soap in there. You just wash up all you can, and then finally I ended up with a unit -- in fact the unit _____ + I was on this train by myself with all these broken German people on the train, and I didn't speak a word of German, especially they give me this little translation book, you know, that you look up and try to say things and ended up where there was nothing standing in that town. Everything was completely wiped out, train station, all it was was just one little stretch of concrete where they had a sign up there that said __________+. So I -- when I got off there I find somebody who spoke English, but nobody spoke English, and there was a guy with this kind of a uniform on and some German, you know, I tried to make myself understood where I was looking for the American outfit out there. He just pointed up that street there, one street, the only one that was cleared up, you know, so I can walk through, so I walked all the way out and left my bag at the so-called station because I can't carry my duffle bag with me, so I left it there and started walking. When I got over the hill and looked down, there was this, sure enough, American Army unit down there, so I walked all the way down there. As I got closer I noticed that everybody was black. In those days, there was segregation. Blacks were put in one company by themselves. Only the officers were white, just like the Civil War, kind of same thing, and so I ended up there, and when I reported to the commanding officer, he said, "You're in the wrong place." He called the headquarters, they said, "Yep, send him back," so back I went. That was my experience, first experience with the Army. I said, Oh, a bunch of stupid people that can't, you know -- if my what I called military occupation, M.O.S. they call it, Military Occupation Specialty, you know, it was considered as I was considered as a draftsman, so that's, in that outfit, anyway, they needed anybody, you know, a little bit of education, something, and the lieutenant that I got to talking to was telling me that they needed a draftsman real bad, needed me right away and work with them there, doing whatever they need, but the company commander said, "No, you can't stay here," so they shipped me back north again and sent me to some other detachment, so handful of guys there, and I worked with them, and now they had some guys there, see, there was two of us who were draftsmen. They had some civilians over there too, local civilians working with us, so we -- I stayed there for a while, worked with them, and then I got transferred back south again to the unit in a place that really was right next to the displacement center with all those European people that are displaced, you know, they're shifted around, especially the Jewish people, because that camp was a camp where the Nazis were putting people in the ______, people to death, putting them in ovens, gas chambers, so I, you know, at the opportune time I go looking around and I saw the ovens, and, in fact, after a few months, Eisenhower came through with his motorcade. They were visiting that place because they wanted to see that, you know, all those people there and what the Nazis had done to all those people there. It must have been, I don't know, a couple thousand people living there, and they were practically starving, and they steal everything they can from us because, you know, you can't blame them, because those guys are hungry and desperate and they have nothing, nothing to lose, and that's why they were looking for any way they can find something, and somehow they sneak into our -- the place where we were located, and with barbed wire around it and everything else, but it meant nothing. They came through somehow and stole everything. But I had one experience where they made me a court-martial clerk where I had the court-martial papers I had to process, and the officers do the prosecuting and all that, you know, military court, you know, court-martials, but I had to do all the work, and then one day this other clerk said, "Hey, look what I got," you know, he had black-marketed -- in those days, cigarettes was the thing to use as money, you know, cigarettes was the thing, so he had, I don't know how many cartons of cigarettes that he had collected and that he had bought this, they call it a Leica, Leica was the best camera then, so they were selling at the PX's and there weren't too many of them so they were rationed and you had to get your ration number in and you wait forever for that, you know, to be able to buy that camera, but anyway, he bought one of those cameras from some displaced person he dealt with, and he came in and said, "Look what I got," you know, bragging about his camera, and then the colonel, the colonel there, the colonel that was doing the court-martialling, he walked in the room and he says, Hey, that's my camera. Where did you get it from?" The guy was stuck. He so shocked he didn't know what to do. He admit it, he said, "Yeah, I got it from this displaced guy that --" he said, "Oh." He says, "Well, since you paid for it, how much I owe you for it?" But the guy didn't want to get court-martialled, so he said, "No, no, no, that's okay, forget about it. You can have it. It's your camera anyway." _________ So he sweated that one out, bullets. But, yeah, that was the experience over there, you know, you didn't know what you were dealing with when you were dealing with those people because they would steal anything they can, and in fact, the mess sergeant we had, he was always giving us, we called it S.O.S., it's -- in those days we called it shit on a shingle, you know. It's some kind of gluey mess that he puts on a slice of toast, you know, and there was nothing else to eat but that, and later on we found out that that guy was black-marketing the rest of the stuff that he was getting in the kitchen, and he was making money off of it. He got caught _____, so he was court-martialled, so I saw all those paperwork come through. That's how I knew about all this kind of stuff. Kept me clean. Kept me honest. I said, Boy, all this stuff, none of that for me, you know, I didn't want to get court-martialled. I got quite an experience out of that, but anyway, then they shipped me out again back north to this Giesen (ph) Quartermaster Depot. That's where I went to and I stayed there till I got my discharge. In fact, the month before I got my discharge, I got this Dear John from my girlfriend back home. Said, Uh-oh, looks like I have nothing to go back home for, so I might as well stay here, so I -- and about that time they got orders for me to report to Berlin because at that time the Cold War started already, you know, Germany was cordoned off to the French, the Russians, the Brittish, and us, you know, they got -- and in Berlin was -- Berlin was in the Russian sector and that was cordoned off like that also, you know, put this different place like that and the Russians actually were constantly harassing the rest of us and not letting us do anything, so they blockaded Berlin, you know. They had this rail that used to go through Berlin, bring all the stuff in. They stopped all that, so there was no way to get to Berlin, so finally the American command, anyway the -- what they call the Allies, they got together and then decided to air-lift everything over to Berlin and that's where I ended up in Berlin keeping track of all that, you know, air-lifted equipment going over there, so they had three of us there doing all that compilation of that, you know, stuff, you know, that was being brought in, so they send me over there for that, just before my one month discharge.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: So you were in the Berlin blockade?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: So I was in Berlin doing that.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Wow.

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: And we were working, actually, the Commandant's office, American Commandant's office, and so we were working in his office and we were doing all that, postage charts and all that stuff and keep track of everything on a daily basis so that military people get together to discuss things they can see now what's going on, so they tried to build up a stockpile of 60 days supply of everything, everything, even coal and water, you know, except water _____, but everything else, stockpile it, because they didn't know what Russia is going to do next, but I -- you know, I got shipped back to my company on the day I was supposed to be retired -- discharged, and I got my discharge papers, and like I said, I got nothing to go back home to, so I stayed there, and I took a job with the military, and that's where I started this spare part supply, built it up from there.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Where were you on V.E. Day? Do you remember V.E. Day?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: V.E. Day?

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Victory over Europe?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: V.E. Day was time I just volunteered for the Army, the day before was V.E.D. As soon as that happened, it was maybe a week before then, but anyway, about that time, I was still in Pearl Harbor then.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Do you --

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: V.J. Day, I was in Germany, and it was in the Korean war, when the Korean War started, I was still in Germany then, and I think I was still in the Army yet when the Korean War started.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Do you remember anything specific on those days? Did you -- like, any celebrations you did on those days?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Nothing, nothing special. In fact, I got to know some German people. I had a German girlfriend for a while, but her family, I got along real well, and in fact, I got along more with her mother than I did with anybody else, you know. She was like a mother to me, you know, she treated me real well, and they used to tell jokes in Germany where the war was going on in Korea, and then here I am in Germany, and the Germany joke was that you know why there is Koreans in, in Germany? They want to see the Americans from in front, not from the rear; you know, that kind of stuff, you know, jokingly. That was one of the German jokes. They didn't tell an American that. Since I got to know them so well, that's the kind of joke they tell.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Have you been participating in a veteran's organization? Have you --

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Every time I go to one of those places, like they got several around, and when I go there, I -- I was in the Army and I saw like -- and enlisted men, they have a club, you know, everywhere you go, they had them, and all they have is this drunken brawls, and when I was, you know, young man, I was very religious type and, you know, I didn't want to fool around with any of that stuff. Now I'm here, and I see these organizations, and I get curious, you know, because they keep asking me to come join us, this and that, and I go and look, same thing. Nothing but drunken brawls. That's all it is. You sit around, you drink, you smoke. I can't stand the smoking anyway because I have -- I have a bad allergy, and then they sit there, they got several cans or bottles of empty, you know, beer, whatever they have there, they -- that's all it is. It's, you know, it's chug-a-lug-a-lug and away, and I didn't care for any of that stuff, so I never really -- even today I get requests to join, you know, to join, but I think if a private place where they don't have any of this stuff, where you get to do more interesting things, then, yeah, I would join then. But in a way I can't blame them because, you know, those guys, they did that while they was in the military. In fact, a lot of them that were in combat, you know, they want to enjoy themselves the rest of their lives, fine, but, you know, I'm not going to do that, so I've never got involved in it.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Have you participated in any, like, memorials or ceremonies?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Yeah, like, see, when was the last time I had? I can't remember any. Been so long ago, because after I retired, I, I was so glad to get back home and I did more things around the home than anything else, and my wife is not able to do that anyway, so I can't drag her along, but we join other things, you know, other groups, like living here, you know, ________ + class that they have here, my wife joined the quilting class and, you know, things like that, so we keep in touch with the community rather than with the military-type people. I never got along with those guys even when I was in the Army and very few guys even in the Army that I could get along with because they usually end up in the E.M. club, you know, getting drunk or something, and I just -- I just couldn't take it. I just didn't want to do any of that stuff. I just want to keep myself thinking, so, on my feet, so I don't have to go, you know, somebody hauling me back home because I'm too drunk. I don't like to get in that situation, no. Just the other, last weekend this guy was, exactly my age, we were comparing notes with the military stuff that we did, and he asked me, said, "Well, if you didn't do any of that stuff, why did you join up?" And I heard that before too, see, so but, no, you can end up that way anyway. Not too many of them out there. He can't help it, you know, it's human nature, so maybe I'm too serious because I always keep my -- I like to keep my nose to the grindstone, even when I was working, I always did that, and I taught my children that. That's why they are doing okay now. We don't have any problems. I don't have a problem with them. They're doing fine.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Is there anything else that you want to add that I perhaps haven't asked about?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Well, like that --

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: About your experiences?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Like that time I thought about where they were rounding up all the Japanese-Americans and they put them up in Manzanar, you know, actually my younger son made a film of that. Yeah, he made a film in school and he called it The Prodigal Son. It's about this Japanese family where this one son takes off and goes to Japan because he was being accused of, you know, not being an American, and he insists that he wasn't going to be treated like that, sent to Manzanar, so he ended up going back to Japan, and in his older years he comes back to visit his father because he's on his death bed, comes back here and get together with the family, and, you know, he hadn't seen him all that time, and he did a pretty good job of that. In fact, he got a lot of awards for that, for that film too, through the USC, so at least my son got a little appreciation of part of what that kind of things that were happening during the war. Even now where they are having this thing about the Arabs, you know, they -- because of this terrorism, mostly Arabians anyway, and some people are blaming all the Arabs of being like that, which isn't true, you know, and that's the kind of relationship I see between that war, in fact, and now where we're fighting this war; those kinds of things, you know, is history repeating itself. Same things coming up again. It's human beings, you know, they are no good at it, so at least I know that my kids understand that because I've talked a lot about my experiences. In fact, they got kind of tired of hearing me talk about it. They said, "Yeah, yeah, Dad, yeah, yeah, Dad, you said it before, Dad," you know.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Were there any social or cultural things you remember of that time period? Like, did you do a lot of swing dancing or any popular --

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Well, I wasn't the dancing one. My sister was. They had the U.S.O. they call it, so she used to go to those things a lot because she liked to dance. In fact, before she died, she always bragged about being a dancer. In fact, we're standing in line, and for certain unknown -- for some unknown reason she said to the person behind her, you know, "I'm a dancer," you know. I looked at her. I said, "What's wrong with her?" No, I wasn't that type. I didn't -- I got too involved in the church when I was a teenager. I became a born-again Christian, that kind of thing. The Army taught me that there isn't such a thing as born-again Christian, you know. You learn. I mean, you learn all the hard knocks of life when you're in the Army. That Army, anyway, when I was in. Today is so, you know, different, like hearing stories about the Army, get an education. Heck, when I was in the Army, there was a lot of guys who didn't even get a high school education, you know, and, boy, they cause all kind of trouble, and being a company court-martial clerk for a while, in fact, I became a company clerk too and was doing all that because there wasn't enough work for a draftsman anyway, so they put me doing all that type of thing, and I learned a lot about guys getting in trouble, various ways, and some of the ways you can't even dream of that they do, really, you know, really, and some of those guys, they come from like areas like we used to call them hillbillies, you know, like Arkansas and those hilly countries, you know, in our country and no education, nothing whatsoever, not even grammar school, some of them can't even write. In fact, I had a first sergeant, the only reason he was a first sergeant was because he was tall, big, tall, muscular, big guy, and nobody could put up with him because if he caused trouble you had to get in a fight with him, and being as big as he was, you know, there was no competition, you know, you ended up in a hospital or something, and that's why he was a first sergeant, because I write up what they call the morning report. Every day that was the -- that was the record for the company, you know, the one you send in every day to headquarters and all the company's records are kept, and because like the men that are in the company, who they are, what they are doing, the job and all that, so it's all in the morning report, and I had to keep track of that, so I finished that up every morning, and first sergeant would come in and he'd sign that, you know. He barely could sign his name, but he had to sign that thing because that's his job. He's supposed to be doing the report, but since he can't do it, I type it up for him, and he puts his -- he doesn't know what I put in there. I could put anything in there. I could have all kinds of stuff in there that shouldn't be there and he wouldn't know the difference. He can't read it anyway, so he just sign it, you know. That's how the Army was then, you know, all kinds of guys like that in there and the officers, oh, we had -- so I would be in the officer's room, and I would do all the paperwork that they have. About 3:00, 4:00 in the afternoon, the company commander come in and he kind of read things quickly, what had to be signed, and sign it and give orders, take off, that's it, and I not see him anymore. Next day, same thing again, and this goes on and on and on, so, same thing with the first sergeant, like I say, he can't read anything anyway. He just come in there and say, "Everything okay, John?" I say, "Yeah, okay," so that's it. And I, you know, I made out the K.P. roster, the guard roster, and, you know, different details, they call it, for the guys to do different things, so I have to make all that up. The company commander come in, he says, Tomorrow we need some of the guys to do this, do that, so I have to pick out the names, you know, type out the hours, post them, and the guys think, you know, hey, the company commander picked their names. Actually I did. They said, "Why you got me doing this shitty detail ________?" Sometimes I didn't like some person, I put them on the work details, and they get mad at the company's commander or the first sergeant or somebody. It's all me doing it. Yeah, it was really something. I couldn't do __________. But that was the Army then, you know. I don't know what they did when they were in the combat companies, where they got out and actually fight. Did you see that last movie, Saving Private Ryan? Did you see that?

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: You can imagine those guys, you know, they are assigned this detail to go find him, and they are going all over the different places and going just about anywhere you can imagine and looking for that guy. Now, how is the company clerk or commander going to keep track of those guys? You know, they are going around and doing this, you know, it's amazing. It was the war. Really something.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: One last question. Is there any details you can remember of specifically what unit you were in?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: What?

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: What unit you were in?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Just for the record, what specifically, what unit you were in?

sp.speaker: John Kim
sp.p: Yeah, when I signed on, they said you can pick the branch of service and command area. So my command area was European Command, _______+ engineering corps, they called it, so I was in the corps, but what job they assign you is up to the place where you end up in, you know, called the company, different companies, so the company I ended up with depends on the commanding officer of that unit, and he can put you anywhere he feels like, but they usually go by, they call it military occupation, your M.O.S., that is your, your given, because when you go into the -- first thing they do is when you get into the Army, basic training, you have to take a test. They call it Army General Classification Test, AGCT, and from there, then they determine what kind of a job you can do, you know, and then they put that M.O.S. under it. Because I tried -- I was doing -- helping them do that too when I was in basic training, so that's why I was, you know, I practically assigned myself as a draftsman because I did that type of work anyway, and like I said, I picked a unit under the area, you know, in Europe and also the branch of service, they call it, engineers, so with the Engineer Corps. In fact, the unit corps that we were in, when I was, when I finally ended up in the end unit, the company, I was in Munich, we were fixing a hospital, a bombed-out hospital building, and our company's job was to rebuild the hospital, so we were using the local laborers, naturally, and they were doing the work and our military people were just kind of supervising, make sure everything was being done right, and then, see, we draw the plans, you know, whatever has to be done and turn it over to the ground field units, and they supervise the work and make sure it's followed, whatever, you know, was put on the paper, so that's how we got the work done, things got done, and a lot of that stuff is what we call military standard operating procedure. We call it S.O.P's. You've got to follow that, so that's what they base the structure on, S.O.P's., so we did most of it that way, and when I -- finally the last unit I ended up in was Riesling (ph), Germany, the Quartermaster Depot, that was old German command post where we took it over, and they even had barracks in there, and it was all built up for the German soldiers, so we occupied that and then started the depot itself. It wasn't any kind of a depot. We just kind of took over the buildings that were there and build them up and make them into a depot for quartermastering equipment and material, whatever you have to store, just from there we would ship it out to the field units throughout the command, you know. Orders come in, ship it out, bring it in from the mainland U.S. and store it there and distribute it from there, so we had to build all that, even the -- there was a lot of concrete work that had to be done too that in Germany it is always rainy and wet, and it would take forever, you know, for concrete to dry, but the Germans had a technique, you know, they can pour concrete and eventually it would dry, but we had to use their system to do that with, because the system that Americans had wouldn't work over there, so, you know, that kind of stuff you had to apply their, their knowledge, so this kind of thing that is so different in working with the field, wherever you are you had to be different. Italy was different again, see, because Italy is like California. It's a different kind of atmosphere, drier, sunnier, not as much water, rain, that kind of thing. It's all different, wherever you go, so that's the kind of stuff I learned as I went along in the military. It was -- I guess where you end up is what you're going to learn from working with that area, you know, not that you bring knowledge with you to do that work over there, but this is going to be different. That's what I learned about because like coming from Hawaii, I know certain things we do in Hawaii that you couldn't do in California, you know, because I walked around in shorts and T-shirt all day long when I was a kid, you know, growing up, but you can't do that here. You wear that type of clothes, you go around like that, might think you were nuts. It doesn't work that way. Same kind, you know, of thing applies everywhere you go, and I found that more and more as I traveled going different places.

sp.speaker: Tony Kim
sp.p: Okay. Well, thank you very much.
